content.figure_caption: Figure 2: Key factors contributing to haemodynamic collapse and death in acute pulmonary embolism (modified from Konstantinides et al. with permission).
content.figure_description: Diagram showing increased RV afterload leading to RV dilatation, TV insufficiency, increased RV wall tension, neurohormonal activation, myocardial inflammation, increased RV O2 demand, intrapulmonary A-V shunting, RV ischaemia/hypoxic injury, reduced RV contractility, decreased RV output, reduced LV preload, decreased cardiac output and systemic BP, reduced coronary perfusion and RV O2 delivery, culminating in obstructive shock and death.
content.main_text: In view of the above pathophysiological considerations, acute RV failure is defined as a rapidly progressive syndrome with systemic congestion resulting from impaired RV filling and/or reduced RV flow output, and is a critical determinant of clinical severity and outcome in acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Clinical symptoms and signs of overt RV failure and haemodynamic instability indicate a high risk of early (in-hospital or 30 day) mortality. High-risk PE is defined by haemodynamic instability and encompasses the forms of clinical presentation shown in Table 4. High-risk PE requires emergency diagnostic (upon suspicion) and therapeutic (upon confirmation or if suspicion is sufficiently high) strategies as outlined in section 7. Absence of haemodynamic instability does not exclude beginning or progressing RV dysfunction and elevated PE-related early risk; further assessment (sections 5 and 7) is necessary to determine level of risk and adjust management.
content.notes: Figure footnote: 'The exact sequence of events following the increase in RV afterload is not fully understood.' Links referenced: Konstantinides et al., and internal section/table references (Table 4; sections 5, 7).
